_comment: Declared policy for what the dotnet feedstock tracks. Human-owned: the
automation reads this and never edits it. Everything the bot cannot decide
for itself is decided here, or escalated as a GitHub issue.
Why this file exists: the workflow used to hardcode `channel: ['10.0']` in a
matrix, which meant .NET 11 and 12 would ship and the bot would stay silent
forever while still reporting success. Blindness that looks like health.
A conda-forge feedstock publishes ONE `dotnet` package, so tracking a new
release line means leaving the old one. That is a judgment call about what
users of a scientific packaging channel want, not something metadata can
answer -- hence `policy` below, and hence new lines become issues, not PRs.
_tracked_comment: Release line -> the upstream feedstock branch that ships it.
This feedstock maintains several lines at once. Upstream branches are
main v2 v3 v5 v6 v7 v8: when a new line takes over `main`, the previous one
gets a `vN` branch so it can keep receiving patches. conda-forge accumulates
every published version, so users can pin `dotnet=8`.
Each tracked line is planned and bumped independently against its own
branch, so concurrent bumps never conflict.
EOL lines (v3, v5, v6, v7) are deliberately absent: they sit at their
final released versions and Microsoft will publish no more, so there is
nothing to detect and watching them would only add noise.
_policy_comment: What we WANT to track, used to judge whether a NEWER channel than anything
lts    - only Long Term Support lines (3 yr). 10.0 is LTS, 11.0 is STS.
latest - newest active line regardless of support type.
manual - never escalate; only bump what is already in `tracked`.
Separately, and regardless of policy: a line that is still supported
(active or maintenance) but absent from `tracked` gets escalated as a
maintenance gap. 9.0 is exactly that today -- it was published as 9.0.203
from main, then 10.0 replaced it and no v9 branch was ever cut, so it is
orphaned nine patch releases behind with no branch to update it from.
_issue_repo_comment: Where judgment-call issues get filed. Defaults to this repo rather than the
feedstock so an unattended bot does not post into a shared conda-forge repo.
Point it at conda-forge/dotnet-feedstock if you would rather co-maintainers
see them -- the token needs issues:write there if you do.
_rid_map_comment: Microsoft RID -> conda-forge subdir. Used to audit which architectures
Microsoft offers against which the recipe actually packages. The set the
recipe packages is NOT duplicated here; it is read from PLATFORMS in
update-dotnet-version.py so the two cannot drift.
A RID mapped here is *mappable*, not necessarily *viable* -- see
_ignore_rids_comment: RIDs with no usable conda-forge equivalent. conda-forge has no musl subdir,
so those can never be packaged and should not generate recurring noise.
_active_subdirs_comment: conda-forge subdirs that are actively built. This is the PRIMARY viability
gate and it is declared, not inferred, because inference got it wrong:
The repodata-size heuristic alone passed win-32 (10.4 MB, 24,464 packages),
but conda-forge stopped building win-32 in 2019 -- newest package there is
dated 2019-02-20. Size distinguishes 'has an ecosystem' from 'empty', but
not 'thriving' from 'frozen and abandoned'. Detecting that from timestamps
would mean downloading repodata (432 MB for linux-64), which CI cannot do.
So: a subdir must be listed here AND pass min_repodata_bytes. Keep this in
sync with what conda-forge actually builds.
_viability_comment: A conda-forge subdir existing is not the same as it being usable. Learned
the hard way on issue #115: linux-armv7l is a real subdir whose repodata is
1,306 bytes -- 3 packages, no icu/openssl/zlib -- so a dotnet built there
would install and be unusable. win-arm64's repodata is ~777 KB (1,927
repodata.json Content-Length is a deliberately cheap proxy for ecosystem
size: one HEAD request, no download. linux-64's repodata is ~432 MB, so
actually fetching these to count packages is not an option in CI.
It is a heuristic, not a guarantee.
